utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Plejo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a reminder, you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony, to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth, okay? Remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm perfectly aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Your last three questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Plejo.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the police was able to enter the district prison in Knin, according to the existing procedure?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police could not enter. Only when they had apprehended a person, were bringing the person in, they would come to the entrance, to the gate, actually. There was a room there to which they would bring arrested persons, but they could not go into the prison proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could the police take out prisoners, inmates, detainees from the prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they could not take the prisoners out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question refers to three persons: Captain Dragan, Mr. Vasiljkovic; Mr. Mladic; Mr. Martic. Did they come to the prison? Did they have access to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the three persons referred to ever came to the district prison in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My very last question. Some witnesses here have told us that they had heard from the prison guards, the prison staff, that some of those persons had, indeed, come to the prison.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm here under oath, and I assert responsibly that no one of these three persons ever came to the prison, to the district prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that ends my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it you, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Plejo. My name is Alex Whiting and I am one of the Prosecutors in the case.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to start with a few questions about your position as warden. You testified that you were the warden in the prison in Knin from August of 1991 until approximately October of 1992, with one brief interruption when Nikola Kukavica was the warden. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that as warden you had contact with the Minister of Justice, Mr. Matkovic, and that you would propose things to him and he would accept those things; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Matkovic knew that you were the warden of the prison from the beginning in August of 1991; right? He knew that.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. Your Honours, I had not been warden before that. The district prison in Knin was set up at that time and I was its warden from the moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From August of 1991. You were appointed in August of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were appointed by Mr. Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Jovica Novakovic was not the warden, was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not the warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He was never the warden, was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to your position as warden. You testified that the chief of the guards, which was first Jovica Novakovic and then it was Ilija Tauz, had to report to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. He was my subordinate. I could not replace him, because the minister was the one who had appointed him and the minister was the one who could replace him, at my proposal of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question was only about reporting, so just please focus on my question and just answer my question. You testified that it was your duty to institute disciplinary proceedings in the event rules were broken; correct? You could initiate disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't have to refer to me as "Your Honours." Now, you also explained that the disciplinary proceedings would be handled by a disciplinary commission, but that you, as the warden, had the final say. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So that means that if there was abuse in the prison in 1991 and 1992, on a daily basis, if there were inadequate conditions for prisoners at that prison in Knin, if the police of the SAO Krajina was permitted to come into the prison to beat and abuse prisoners, then you could be held responsible for that as warden of the prison, couldn't you? If those things occurred and you did nothing about it, then you could be held responsible; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in that case, I would be responsible. But the police never was allowed to come into the prison and beat --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You have answered my question.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You answered my question. In fact, you could be criminally prosecuted if those things happened under your watch and you did nothing about it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I could have been criminally prosecuted, but I could have certainly been replaced from the position of warden, had such things indeed happened, had people from the outside come into the prison. But they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you're not aware that you -- if those things happened under your watch, you knew about them, you did nothing to prevent them or punish them, you could be criminally prosecuted as a war criminal. You're not aware of that? You know that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not shirking from that. I did everything that I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could answer my question, please. You know that if those things happened under your watch, you knew about them and you just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has replied once. My colleague, the Prosecutor, can of course ask the same question a million times, but that is badgering the witness. It is not the Prosecutor's task here to intimidate witnesses. So what kind -- how many times is he going to ask the witness whether he was a war criminal in order to obtain the answer that he wants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whether he was a war criminal? Sorry, I don't understand that last statement, Mr. Milovancevic. "How many times is he going to ask the witness whether he was a war criminal in order to obtain the answer that he wants?" The witness said he didn't know that he could be criminally charged, and I think that last sentence, the last point, that last statement is properly asked. Others perhaps may not be, I don't know. But let's hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just pressing the witness, I think hardly badgering him, just pressing him on that last answer, that he claimed that he didn't know whether he could be criminally prosecuted. So I was just putting the question to him one more time, to press him a little bit on that. I don't think I was badgering him. And I certainly wasn't asking him if he was a war criminal. Just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I fully understood that. Okay. That last question on whether he was -- he knew that he could be criminally charged as a war criminal can be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- I apologise, Your Honours. I have to reply to the answer given by my learned colleague, the Prosecutor. This question would be logical if the witness had said that "I know that I would be responsible had that happened, but it did not happen." But this is something that the Prosecutor is failing to take into consideration. He continues to pursue his thesis along the lines, what -- would you be a war criminal had that really happened? That is what I mean. Perhaps the witness has said something more than the Prosecutor asked him, but he definitely did say, "No, this did not happen while I was warden." And this is l'art pour l'art on the part of the Prosecutor. What would have happened had something else been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I rule that you may ask that question, Mr. Whiting, that last question on whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, if you could answer my question, please. You know that if those things happened - abuse in the prison, inadequate conditions, beatings by SAO Krajina police - if those things happened in the prison in Knin under your watch and you knew about it and you did nothing to prevent it, you know, don't you, sir, that you could be criminally prosecuted for that as a war criminal; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you answer, sir, just so that that question is not asked again, listen to the question and answer directly to the question and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, please, or do you want me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you don't have to repeat the question. I have understood it. Mr. Prosecutor, it is possible for anyone to become a war criminal in war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, because your counsel wants to make sure that things are not repeated. Now, answer the question and answer just the question, nothing less, nothing more. We don't want to know whether you understand that it is possible for anyone to become a war criminal. Answer the question directly, once and for all, and let's move on to the next point. The answer is either, "Yes, I do know," or "No, I don't know," or "No." It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move back in time to the beginning of your testimony when you talked about working at Tvik factory in Knin. You testified that one day the Croatian -- the Croat employees did not show up to work. In the summary of your evidence that was provided to us by the Defence, it says that this event occurred in 1991, that the Croat employees did not show up to work. Is that right? Did it occur in 1991?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me that the population in the Knin municipality was approximately 92 per cent Serb and 8 per cent Croat; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that in July of 1990, Milan Martic and others initiated a petition within the police in Knin which was against the new patch that was being proposed on the uniform. Are you aware of that, sir? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was exactly like that. At that time I was working at Tvik, and I had no contact with the police. I had nothing to do with the police whatsoever. I was doing -- I was working at this factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, my question was whether you heard about it. Did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know that in August of 1990, Milan Martic said on television that the people's police in Knin would not listen to the Croatian government? This is Exhibit 4 and 5, Your Honours. Did you hear that on television? Did you see that on television?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were living in Knin at the time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 5 or 6 kilometres away from Knin; 5 to 6 or perhaps 10 kilometres, in the vicinity of Knin more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What village were you living in, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you weren't following the events with the barricades and the pronouncements coming out of the police and what was happening in the media, in August of 1990?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned to the -- you mentioned the barricades. I followed the goings on with the barricades, because they were put up also in my village by the villagers, and that had nothing to do with this first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you didn't follow in the media the pronouncements that were coming -- that were being made by some of the leaders in Knin, like Milan Martic, Milan Babic? You weren't following those things?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The barricades, were you involved with them yourself; that is, did you participate in setting them up or manning them?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all participated. We all participated together, we, the villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Putting aside whether they were set up spontaneously or not, you know, don't you, that within days the barricades were organised and managed by the Council for National Resistance? You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it was managed by anyone. This was a spontaneous exercise by the villagers, and virtually the villagers of every village put up barricades. I don't believe that they were managed in an organised fashion by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're telling us that after they were put up, that in August and September, in October, in November, December of 1990, they continued to be unorganised and unmanaged? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so. There was a barricade also in the place where I lived, and I just told you that I lived some 7 or 8 kilometres away from Knin, but believe me, barricades were also put up 2 kilometres outside of Knin, so that I, myself, couldn't pass through. We were afraid. We only watched HTV, which is to say Croatian television at that time, and we were afraid that there were threats. So that people erected these barricades in their own villages in fear, for their own safety, that of their neighbours and of their kin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question. You're maintaining that, to your knowledge, there was nobody organising or commanding the barricades during all of 1990, after August? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the municipality of Knin is a large one. Now, whether someone did participate or not is something that I don't know. I don't know of any names. But I'm talking about my village, where I know the barricades were put up spontaneously by the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question to you is: Is that your testimony? Just listen to the questions. We don't want to be repeating questions. Listen to the question and answer the question. Was that your testimony? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, now you have told us that you don't really know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Whiting. You have been asked a question: Is that your testimony? I would like an answer to that. If you want to know what is your testimony, he can repeat the question. But the question was: Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I understood the question properly, the Prosecutor asked me who managed those barricades. I believe that I have answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was: "You are maintaining that, to your knowledge, there was nobody organising or commanding the barricades during all of 1990, after August. That is your testimony?" That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have replied that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your reply is that you don't know that it's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I said is that, in my village, no one organised the barricades. As regards places 50 kilometres away from my home, how should I know whether someone organised them or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were being asked about your village, sir. I said listen to the questions and listen to them very attentively. The question to you, and I repeat: "Are you maintaining, sir, that, to your knowledge, there was nobody organising or commanding the barricades during all of 1990, after August? Is that your testimony?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified about the clash in Plitvice, that "a couple of my friends or neighbours from the place, from my place, were also at Plitvice and they were on the Krajina police force." That's at page 27 of yesterday's transcript. So the clash at Plitvice was between members of the Krajina police force, including some officers from Knin and the Croatian MUP. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at Plitvice myself. I only know a man who was, a friend of mine was there. I cannot tell you in what capacity he was there. I know that after having finished his military service he was on the reserve police force. I, myself, was not at Plitvice and don't know anything about the clashes, except what I heard about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, yesterday what you said was that "a couple of my friends," not "friend," but "a couple of my friends or neighbours from my place were at Plitvice and they were on the Krajina police force." So you know that members of the Krajina police force from your area were at Plitvice; right? That's what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just referred to one person. Later, I came to know some people and we became friends, and from talking to them I heard that they had been at Plitvice. That is perhaps why yesterday I said several of my friends. But these were a couple of friends whom I only got to know later. And before the clash at Plitvice, I only knew one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. What's the name of the one that you knew before the clash? What's his name?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Vujakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the names of the others that you learned later were at Plitvice, what are their names?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly right now. I just remember the first names. There was a Milan and a Jovan, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You really can't remember their last names?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot. You see, sir, it was a brief period and people made friends quickly. We would often have a coffee together without even knowing each other's names. If we were to meet even now, we would have a drink together. But we really didn't know each other's surnames.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. You testified that after Plitvice, you were invited or you were summonsed by Milan Martic to join the reserve force of the SAO Krajina police, and that you accepted. Now, when that occurred, you had no experience in police and no training as a policeman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no previous experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And no training; right? You had not been trained in any way to be a policeman; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no training for a policeman. But I served the army before, and after doing military service, people would become members of the police or of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just listen to the question and answer the question. You were given -- after you accepted, you were given equipment, weapons, a uniform and a police vehicle; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kinds of weapons were you given?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a pistol of Zastava make. I believe that the calibre was 7.62, and that is the pistol that all of the police were issued with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what other weapons?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: An automatic rifle, as issued to each policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who gave you these things, these weapons?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I reported to the police station, I was registered as a reservist and then the procedure followed on --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. Give me the name of the person who gave you these weapons.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the name. It was probably the employee who was in charge of those affairs at the SUP. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. After approximately 20 days, you were told to report to Golubic; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who told you to report to Golubic? The name, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same thing again. I was called up from the SUP. It was probably the duty officer who was on duty at the SUP at the moment, conveying me a message. And I don't know the name of the person. I knew very few people at the SUP at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You described the training that you received at Golubic as "classical police training." This is at page 33 of yesterday's transcript. How do you know what classical police training is?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I not know? You see that sort of thing all the time on television. I was also an active soldier during my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was rather dissimilar to the training -- to the drills that you had in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, okay. So what you've described as classical police training is, in fact, similar to training that you received in the army. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said exactly the opposite. It's not similar to what you get in the army. The army provides training involving a different kind of weaponry. I said exactly the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Line 12, page 15 has a record completely the opposite to what the witness said. It says: "It was rather similar," and the witness said it was rather dissimilar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's what the witness has just been explaining, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's on the record, that mistake. The witness said completely the opposite, and this is not the first time that wrong things are recorded. I would appreciate it if the interpreters could take greater care. The interpreters cannot be a party to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This was a genuine mistake and a very rare one. The words in our language are very similar, sound very similar. It was obviously not intentional, and this comment was absolutely uncalled for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Interpreter. Mr. Milovancevic, I'm saying to you, the witness heard that, he was in the process of correcting it with counsel, and I don't think -- I want to endorse what the interpreter is saying: Your comment is uncalled for so far as it relates to them, because it is -- it may not be the first mistake they are making but it is not a regular mistake. It is a very rare mistake. And I think they're working here under great pressure, like all of us, and I think we must give them the due respect and the due credit for what they do. Mr. -- Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, Your Honour, and I appreciate that. Excuse me just a minute. Let us clear this up. The question of the Prosecutor was very brief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the answer is, "how do you know that it was" -- Your Honour, it's a very important matter. The witness provided a very brief, precise answer that cannot be, in any way, interpreted or misinterpreted to sound quite the opposite. I proceed from the same language that the interpreters hear, so it's unfathomable how something like this could be put on the record. It's a complete inversion of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, is it your suggestion that the interpreter deliberately misquotes the witness? Just put it clearly and unambiguously. Is that what you're suggesting? Because I don't know the language that you speak. I am not able to judge whether that mistake could or could not have been made. If you say, the question was so simple and the answer was so simple and straightforward that it could not be mistakenly misinterpreted, are you suggesting that, therefore, the interpreters did that deliberately? Now, if that is your suggestion, file a complaint, Mr. Milovancevic, and let's deal with the interpreter. Is that your suggestion, sir, that the interpreter is deliberately misinterpreting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was only trying to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you a direct question, Mr. Milovancevic. Are you suggesting that the interpreter is deliberately misinterpreting? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. This was impossible to interpret the way it was interpreted. If the man says military training was different from police training and they say it was the same, I don't know how that could happen. Otherwise, let them take greater care, what they're doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I ask you a question now: What are you going to do about it? You have made an allegation that the interpreter deliberately misinterprets you. What do you want to do about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You cannot do nothing about it. You are going to have to do something about it. That's a very serious allegation you are making, sir. We are going to have to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is our choice. By publicly drawing the attention -- your attention to the problem, I did what I wanted. I wanted to produce an effect, and that effect has been produced. I don't want to continue publicly accusing anyone of anything. I just want everybody -- everybody who knows -- who is doing this work knows that this is being recorded and that we are following the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Milovancevic, I do not agree with you. You have made a very serious allegation against the Prosecutor, and I think if the Prosecutor is found to have done so intentionally -- I beg your pardon. What am I saying? If the interpreter is found to have done something intentionally, she has to be dealt with according to the regulations of this institution, and you will have to come and substantiate your case before the people. I will have to ask for the name of the interpreter. May I please get the name of the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No, Judge, I beg you to allow me to speak. Mr. Milovancevic, I would like to think that the words came out of your mouth before you could stop them, and with hindsight, you regret the statement which was made in the heat of the moment. And to challenge the integrity of a professional, technical professional person is very, very serious. And we know how hard the interpreters work to keep up with the pace to fulfil their duties with integrity. Please do withdraw the statement and let us move on. The effect that you intended, I don't know whether it will actually be what is the reality. But in the circumstances, I believe the statement was unfortunate, and the honourable thing to do is to withdraw it. I give you the opportunity now. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept fully what you say, Honourable Judge Nosworthy, and I withdraw my statement. I just want to explain that the reason for this reaction of mine may have been something that happened on Friday that Mr. Martic drew my attention to, and I withdraw my statement in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm sorry to have intervened, Mr. Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You have done that with Judge Nosworthy. Interpreter, can I have your name, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, you know, I just wonder if that should be done in private session. I mean the identity of interpreters is usually protected at the Tribunal. So if it is going to be disclosed, I think maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will ask, then, that the interpreter give me their name later. Mr. Milovancevic, I do not accept your withdrawal for the simple reason that it is suggested by somebody else, that it hasn't come from you. I am going to believe that is what you genuinely feel. I will demand that you deal with this matter as you have claimed. You have said -- you have challenged the integrity of an interpreter here, and you were asked very clear, before you could give me an explicit answer, I asked you, "Is that what you are suggesting," that it was intentionally done. And I want you to substantiate that. Okay? So, notwithstanding what Judge Nosworthy has said, you are going to have to deal with this matter, all right? I have seen the interpreter who is speaking. Even if I don't have her name, I will be able to do so. I will file a report with the President, and you will have to deal -- take it from there. I don't know who deals with these things, okay? Now -- yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I accepted the suggestion of Her Honour Judge Nosworthy, I did it as a professional, with full responsibility and completely consciously. The fact that I had thought that can be proved very simply by what I said earlier, that I don't want to pursue the issue any further, that I produced the effect desired by publicly pointing to the problem. I gave that answer at your insistence. Now, your insistence, Your Honour Judge Moloto, brings me into an embarrassing position, Judge Nosworthy and the entire Trial Chamber, because I'm accepting this as a suggestion from an equal member of the Trial Chamber and I accepted it as a suggestion of the Court. In my eyes, it is a matter of indifference whether it was said by the Presiding Judge or Judge Hoepfel or Judge Nosworthy. I was addressed by the Court, and in communicating with the Court, I said, "This is my position." As for this problem, I will gladly provide an explanation why I reacted in this way, but I don't think it would be advisable to go into this procedure. On Friday, I stopped Mr. Martic from saying things that he overheard from the interpreters. Now, I apologise to the interpreter concerned now by withdrawing my statement. I don't think the matter should be raised further, and I am now appealing to the Trial Chamber not to insist any further. I had my reasons for pointing to this problem, and I did it in a way that I wanted to be very serious. I didn't intend any contempt of court and I didn't want to level unjustified accusations against anybody or question anybody's integrity. Many people are taking turns working here. I know they have a very hard job, and I respect it, but also respect my job, and my job as Defence counsel is to monitor how words are being interpreted. If something is interpreted to mean exactly the opposite of what was said, then it is very serious. I would please appreciate it if we couldn't -- if we wouldn't pursue this matter any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you are embellishing your own statements. You are now claiming that you have apologized to the interpreter by withdrawing the statement. Withdrawing the statement is one thing; apologising to the interpreter is completely another matter. You have not done so, sir, let me tell you that; number 1. Number 2, when you answered Judge Nosworthy, and now in this last statement you are still trying to justify why you did it because of what happened on Friday. What happened on Friday, I asked you, what is Mr. Martic saying? You said you would rather not say. You said you didn't want to go into it. I asked you a second time and you said you didn't want to go into it. If you would have raised it, we would have dealt with it. But I do not want to believe that what you heard on Friday, which I don't know anything about, has anything to do with the interpretation. If this interpreter is -- unless you are going to say that this is the same interpreter who said -- who did what you say you heard on Friday, I do not know that, and I do not want to go into that and I do not intend linking these two things. But you're using what happened on Friday as justification to mean that you are not remorseful about what you have done, and that is endorsed by the very fact that you have not expressly apologized to the witness -- to the interpreter, rather. This record is standing here. There is no way I can delete it. I must deal with this matter to its finality. The only way to do so, sir, is that you face up to this interpreter in a proper forum and deal with this matter. And for purposes of these proceedings, I don't want that later you come and say here, "I'm appealing because some interpreters were misinterpreting my witnesses." If this interpreter, as you say, is deliberately misinterpreting, then she must be taken off from this case. I want the interpreter who is going to do the job and do it properly so that there are no irregularities at the end of the trial. So it is not just a question of you making allegations and then quickly withdrawing them and saying that we must just sweep things under the carpet. I cannot do that. This is a public forum, and, yes, I understand that you are doing your job, and everybody else is here is doing his job and everybody else here is working under great pressure. Now, I will follow this matter up. I will make a report to the President, and I will ask that the matter be investigated so that this interpreter be removed from my trial, if she is found to deliberately misinterpret witnesses. Now, I don't think we need to go into dialogue about this. If you have anything to say, say it very briefly. Let's carry on with the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be very brief. You say that what happened on Friday is being used by me to justify what happened today. But you don't know what happened on Friday, and I do. And that's the only reason why I linked it up with today's context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are telling us that -- you are saying to Judge Nosworthy why you reacted the way you did today is because of what happened on Friday. For me, you are not truly remorseful about what you have done today. You are justifying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I will have this resolved publicly. I will apologise to the interpreter concerned today. I will say it publicly. I don't think it is necessary to burden you any further or the President of the Tribunal or anybody else. My withdrawal of that statement a moment ago was perfectly sincere. I am doing it now, Your Honour. I apologise to the lady interpreter for the sentence that I uttered. I withdraw my words and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: To make you understand, Mr. Milovancevic, how serious this is, you also stated this was not the first time, and you are, by that, jeopardising the reputation of the Tribunal. I find it a very serious issue, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are talking about interpreters and a specific error. When I mentioned previous cases, those were mistakes concerning dates, digits, numbers, that are easily explained. And I did not intend to question the integrity of the Tribunal, nor did I have that intention in making my comment today. This is a technical issue. We cannot work without interpretation. Since there was a specific sentence concerned, I had to react, and I think if I created a problem before the Trial Chamber, I regret it. That was not my intention. It was not my intention to object against the Trial Chamber or the Prosecutor or the Tribunal as a whole. I was just dealing with a specific problem, a specific misinterpretation, and I apologized, Judge Hoepfel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you for saying that, but I wouldn't agree that you've just dealt with this specific problem. You made that generalisation, and that is a very dangerous allegation. You said this was the opposite, the exact opposite of what originally was said, and this was not the first time. That weighs very heavily. So, I think we are in a real problem. And you said something about an intention you had to cause a certain effect, and having been successful in causing this effect. What did you mean by that? You didn't make that clear, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my entire address concerning this misinterpretation, I was very specific. I meant the job of the person who is doing the interpreting, and when I said I produced an effect, I wanted to say that by pointing publicly to the problem of interpretation, I warned the specific interpreter to be more careful as to how she interprets. And I thought that by pointing to the problem, I have dealt with it, I resolved it. I didn't want to deprive anyone of their livelihood because of the mistake they made, and I don't think it is necessary to take any further steps. I just wanted to say, when something like this happens, it is serious. That was all I meant. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, one thing would be to substantiate, really, exactly what you meant by saying that was not the first time, because when I asked you, you now said it was not the same, what happened before. You mentioned something about figures which came over just by mistake or something. And so you can explain what this sentence can mean, because it is really a very strong public statement, "This is not the first time."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not the first time in the course of this trial that we had corrections to make in the record, that something was misinterpreted - a date or a number or a specific piece of information. I was just explaining why I reacted the way I did. It's human to err and errors happen. But this was a drastic mistake, in my eyes. It's not like I hit a mountain with my head and I'm reacting for the first time saying it's a problem. Of course there are problems in the normal course of things and they are being dealt with. In this case, tensions are raised because of the insistence that I explain. And I was trying to explain, but my explanation had nothing to do with the whole institution, just the work of a specific person in a specific sentence. I apologised to that person and I withdrew my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: To get you clear on that, Mr. Milovancevic, do you not insinuate that mistakes of translations occurred before in this case without having been addressed by you? So is this not your insinuation? Make that very clear, please. If something happened, we made it clear we corrected it or whatever, because of course mistakes can happen. But it's very important to correct them immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we always reacted to errors in numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- dates. I said it clearly, and to avoid any confusion and to avoid all of the blame landing on me, there was a comment made by the interpreters, a comment, not an interpretation, at my expense and concerning the work of the Trial Chamber that could have raised a doubt in my mind in the objectivity of the interpreters as such. I don't want to raise this issue and I didn't intend to, but by insisting on this error, I wanted to point out to the people who are doing their job, that we read this. Nothing more and nothing less, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Judge? Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to proceed with your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would just note that the error was fully cleared up on the record before Mr. Milovancevic even started to speak, and that's quite clear on the record. The witness clarified it. It was quite clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I did say that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's right. I would also like to note that I -- I mean, I have to say that I am quite shocked by what's happened here. I can only imagine that the interpreter, probably all of the interpreters but certainly the interpreter at issue, is shocked and probably quite distressed by what's occurred here. I don't know if the Court wants to see if the interpreter can continue, if we should take a break, but you know I'm sure this is quite upsetting. So I just raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for raising that, because in fact it's been at the back of my mind that we haven't heard her. We haven't heard whether she accepts the apology or not. And I would like to hear from her, but maybe -- I'm not quite sure whether to ask her whether she needs a break or not, or we should just take a break nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is perfectly all right, Your Honour. We don't like to be the centre of attention anyway, such is the nature of our job. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: She is speaking like the consummate professional that I know and understand her to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. And underlying that consummate professional, there is a human being, with human feelings, which are affected by things that are said and done to her, and it is our responsibility to be sensitive to that. She is not just -- she is not and automatic -- she is a human being with feelings. Now I would suggest we take a break and come back maybe after 15 minutes. We will take a long one. We will come back at the normal time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided to request, as we hereby do, the head of the interpreters to get a transcript of the interpretation that was alleged to have been misinterpreted, listen to the recordings, the original, and give the Chamber a report on her findings. Once the Chamber is in receipt of that report, the Chamber will decide how to take the matter further. For now, it will end at that point and we will carry on with the case. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, before the interruption, you had testified that the training at Golubic was different from the training that you had received when you did your military training. Now, in fact, isn't it true that the training at Golubic in 1991 included military training, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that special units were trained at Golubic and that the intention - and this is, in fact, what occurred - was that the special units would go to places like Knin and Benkovac and Obrovac and would engage in military operations after their training? They were trained to do that.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday what it was that we learned there. What may have been somebody's intention is something that I cannot assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, didn't you learn, wasn't it obvious, at Golubic that there were special units being trained for military operations?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, when I was being trained, I had a feeling that I would be assigned to some VIP security position to secure a municipality president or something similar. I could not conclude on the basis of that that I would be assigned to a war unit, to a war operations unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at Exhibit 622 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we take a look at this exhibit, I must express my concern at answers which do not address the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understood the answer on the last -- with respect to the last question - I don't know if that's the question Your Honour is referring to - that the witness answered that he could not -- it was not obvious to him that there were special units being trained there for military purposes. That's how I understood the last sentence of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but you see the problem is that what he's not able to conclude, namely that he's not able to conclude that he would be assigned to a war, is based not on what is being done at Golubic but on his feeling about what would happen when he went there when you get the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct, Your Honour. I will pursue it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let's not just talk about what happened to you and your feeling. You were trained at Golubic for some 20 days and then you participated yourself in training. Wasn't it obvious to you that there was military training going on there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not obvious to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at this exhibit. This, as you can see, is -- I'm just checking to make sure that the English is up. Yes. As you can see, these are minutes from a meeting on the 14th of June 1991. Now, that was around the time when you were at Golubic; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you mean "possibly"? You were there, weren't you? Not at the meeting. You were at Golubic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was probably in Golubic at that time. I cannot recall the exact date. I have said that I cannot remember exact dates. That is why I ask of you not to ask me to recall whether it was exactly on that date. I may have already been at the old hospital at that time. We talked about that yesterday. I cannot know the -- remember the exact date. I may have left with a group of 15 or 20 people for the old hospital, as we said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But then again I may have been at Golubic. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the memo. You see in the first paragraph that two of the participants are individuals that you've spoken about in your testimony, Dragan Karina and Captain Dragan. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see that the goals of the meeting are "agreement on further work in Golubic; units for covering of outskirts are to be determined; the training of units." Do you see that? One, two, three?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then the next section is: "Agreement on further work in Golubic," and there is what appears to be a list of different units and numbers or different groups. Korenica, Plitvice, Knin group, the Medak, Plaski. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I would like to see the next page on the B/C/S, please, and it's at the bottom of the page in English. Do you see where it says with respect to the Medak group, it says: "People are to be trained in setting mines, destroying roads, setting a deep ambush, trapping into the ambush and defending the ambush. The Glina and Vojnic folks are to be trained in the mining of vehicles, buildings and objects, sniper shooting." If we could turn to the next page in the English. "Plaski: The construction of defensive positions, the blocking of a town, operating with rifle grenade, ambush." Is that what you meant when you described "classical police training"? Are those the things you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Possibly at that meeting - and I don't know anything about the meeting itself, nor do I know the people who attended the meeting - it is possible that they may have adopted such a decision for defence in some outskirts. But we didn't have such training. I know nothing about explosives or setting of mines. Never did I have an explosive device in my hands so never did I know how to operate those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, putting aside how you may have trained or what you held in your hands, that was the training that was going on at Golubic, wasn't it, what is described here in the memo?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that I had that kind of training, the setting of mines, the building of defence positions. I explained to you yesterday what kind of training we received at Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Exhibit 620, please. And before we do, is there some reason that you don't want to disclose the military aspect of the training at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing. I actually did not understand your question, why wouldn't I answer, why wouldn't I say what was going on there. I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's why I put the question to you, because I wanted to know why. Let's look at Exhibit 620, please. This is -- and if we could look at the last page of the exhibit. This is a report, and you see it is the name there at the end and it is signed, you know that is the name of Captain Dragan; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature? I don't know whether it is his signature or not, if you are talking about the signature here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm talking about the name. Daniel Snedden is one of the names used by Captain Dragan; right? You know that.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. This is the first time I hear of that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the first page, then, and I will put to you that this is a report about the training at Golubic in 1991. After number 1, in the first paragraph, it says: "The first group spent 21 days on training." That sounds like your group, doesn't it? Approximately 20 days of training; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "During the training, the programme was stopped only for 36 hours because of an operation in Bratiskovci." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been an interruption. I cannot recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember the operation in Bratiskovci?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remember one operation, the action at Udbina, which I referred to yesterday, and that was, I believe, the only time that I left the camp. Or I just don't remember. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, a little further down, in the beginning of the next paragraph, it says: "It was impossible to train the formation --" the sentence, the translation is a little awkward here, but, "to reach," that's what it is, "to reach the level on which it could act as a unit." And then in the next paragraph, it says: "I am of the opinion that in such a complicated political situation in the country, the only chance to create a unity in our armed forces is to depoliticise the armed units." The training at Golubic, I will put to you, sir, was about training armed units, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I replied with a "no," though it is what you think is your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And seeing this report, your answer is still "no"?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who compiled this report. I'm not that much interested. But I do know that ten people from each municipality cannot really constitute some armed force; that is one thing. And, secondly, I saw those people afterwards, and they were mainly engaged as drivers or as people -- as security guards. So that was the actual output of the training. So I didn't believe that they could constitute an armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Plejo, you're not aware that in the fall of 1991, when you were working at the Knin district prison, that special units of the SAO Krajina police were engaged in military operations? You don't know that? That they would participate with the JNA in military operations?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I worked in the court, how should I know? How could I have known who participated in which operation? I never received any reports as to who was participating in what.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So when you just answered a moment ago about all of these people being trained at Golubic being drivers, you really don't know what they did, do you, in the fall of 1991? That's your answer now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the later period I saw several of those people who had been with me. I saw one of them driving this minister; the other -- another one was securing another minister. And on that basis, I can conclude that that was what the unit was being trained for. As for military operations, it is quite possible that some of them later joined some military units, even on a voluntary basis. That is quite possible. How should I know? Seeing that later I worked in the district prison, how should I know where all of these people were? I knew where my brother and my father were and not where the rest of the people were --.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and, of course, I knew where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt please. Can you please speak slowly, sir. The interpreter is desperately trying to keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you just said: "... it is quite possible that some of them later joined some military units, even on a voluntary basis," that's just pure speculation on your part. You have no idea what happened to these units and whether these men joined voluntarily or were ordered to participate in military operations, do you? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened with those people afterwards and where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So let's look -- let's look at the next page of this document, please, both in the B/C/S and in English. And it states -- in the B/C/S, it's in the upper third of the document, so maybe if we could blow it up for the witness so he could read it. In the English, it's also in the upper third of page 2. It says: "Our main goal should be that people who finish the training would go home and establish many polygons in areas where it is possible, as well as the warehouses, from where the new formations would grow." Didn't you know that that was the goal at Golubic, that the units, these special units, would be trained, they would go back -- they would go back to the village from where they came and create a new formation which would grow there? You knew that, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. How should I have known? It was up there at the fortress. How should I have known what they were planning up there, at the fortress?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, this was with regard to training at Golubic and you were at Golubic. But your testimony is that you don't know about any of these things?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, if I was in Golubic, I was supposed to go back to my native village and create a new unit there. But I didn't do that. I started working for the Ministry of Justice. It may have been somebody's intention for that to happen, but I cannot comment on people's intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm asking about what was happening at Golubic. Those are what my questions are about. Now, you know also at Golubic Frenki Simatovic, maybe known to you only as Frenki, was there, wasn't he, at Golubic? You recognise that name, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki Simatovic is a name that I know from Belgrade. After the bombing campaign, when his name was referred to, when he was arrested and sent to The Hague, that is how I heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't hear his name or see him at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about Mark? Was there a trainer by the name of Mark at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been. I really don't remember the names. I was there for a very short time, for 20 days, and for a part of that period at Udbina with my team. That is a very short time. And then it was 15 years ago. And, as I said, I don't remember names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, when you were being asked questions on direct examination, you didn't have any trouble remembering anything, did you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have trouble remembering first and last names. At that time I wasn't married, I was single, so that I remember more the names of girls. Yesterday I also said that I could not remember dates and names, and especially not the names of these people where I spent only 10 or 15 or 20 days with them. You must appreciate the fact that if one spent just 15 days with some people 15 years ago, that is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we talked about people with whom I had spent about four years in the prison; that's why I remembered their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this must have been a big change in your life. You had been working at Tvik from 1985, you had been working there for six years, and all of a sudden, in April of 1991, you become a reserve policeman. You get a gun; you get a police car; you go to Golubic; you become a trainer at Golubic. Those must have been memorable, significant events in your life; no?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the events. I don't remember the exact dates when they took place and I don't remember the names of the people involved. That is what is difficult for me to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about another trainer by the name of Fico or Fica; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that Milan Martic had authority over the camp at Golubic. He also came to the camp, didn't he? He would actually physically come to the camp; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that Mr. Milan Martic was in charge. When I came to Golubic, my commanding officer, Dragan Karina received me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what you said --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And during those 20-odd days that I spent there, I never once saw Mr. Milan Martic. Whether he came or didn't, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, yesterday - and it is at page 42 of the transcript - His Honour Judge Moloto asked you if Milan Martic had authority over Golubic, and you said, "I suppose so." Are you changing that testimony now?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. But you asked me whether he used to come there. How should I know? I had only just arrived in Golubic. I was introduced to my commanding officer. He showed me my tasks. Why should I know who is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, let me interrupt you. The reason I referred you to your testimony of yesterday is that you said a moment ago, "I didn't say that Mr. Milan Martic was in charge." In fact, your testimony is that he had authority over the camp, he was in charge of the camp; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said maybe. That may mean yes or no. I knew my commanding officer. I had only just arrived and I knew my commanding officer. How should I have known who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- you testified that you were trained at Golubic and that you became a trainer, and that the training was classical police training. Now, you knew that Milan Martic was the secretary of the Secretariat of the Interior at the time. Is there any reason you doubt his authority over the camp training the police?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly why I said maybe. But I don't know that. I had just arrived there. And how should I have known after a day or two who was in charge? I knew my commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, doesn't classical police training include chains of command and how orders are given and who has the authority, things like that? Aren't those things that would be included in that kind of training?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told you who my commanding officer was. Possibly the head of the SUP or the secretary of the SUP or the minister was his superior. I don't know how the vertical chain of command functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police ranks were familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, you're telling us that you actually trained police officers at Golubic without knowing what the chain of command was within the police of the Krajina? That's your testimony? You did not even know what the chain of command was?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I did not know the entire echelons. I knew the commanding officer, the chief. I could not know at that moment who was the commanding officer or my commanding officer. I did not know the entire chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that some men came from Benkovac to be trained; in fact, I think you trained these men from Benkovac. Goran Opacic was one of these men from Benkovac, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Namely, I didn't say that it was I who trained them. I trained people from, I believe, Korenica and a couple of lads from Udbina, where we were in the field. I never stated that we trained people from Benkovac. Ten or 15 guys came from Benkovac, from Obrovac and other municipalities; that is what I said yesterday. I didn't say that I was their commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I misunderstood that part of the testimony, then. But if you could answer my question: The men who came from Benkovac included Goran Opacic, didn't they? He was one of the men from Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know that person personally. I heard that he's an athlete, a karate athlete, but I don't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say you don't know him personally. But did you learn -- did you hear that he was at Golubic at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. He may have been, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that you went to Udbina to do training. If you're doing classical police training, as you've claimed, as you described, why did you have to go to Udbina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, when you get an order, you execute it. You don't ask why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier in the army and in the police, that was the way it was. But I'll tell you now, I assumed it was because the young men who were there were from that area and they said they wanted to go home. And it was not a problem for me to be in there place. And they had accommodation, so it was not a problem for me, and I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now you're telling us that because the people being trained wanted to go home, you said, "All right, fine, we'll go do it in Udbina." That was the reason? Or was it because you received an order to go do it in Udbina? I'm a little confused.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those young men, whose commanding officer I was, they were natives, some of them from Udbina, some from Korenica. They expressed their wish to get training up there, and the commanding officer approved that. Why not spend a couple of days in Udbina so they can see their families? I don't see what it is that you don't understand here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, when you described yesterday some of the training that you did, you included "descending a rope on a rock face." Is that, in your mind, classical police training, descending a rope on a rock face?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not? I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you think so, why? Is that something you saw on TV?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying why wouldn't it be? I didn't have to see it. If it was somebody's assessment that it's a part of the training, why wouldn't it be? I don't see the point of your question. I don't see the difference. And I did see it on television, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, the question is whether that's police training or military training, and you maintain that is police training.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in 1984 I was in the army. In the army, the training was different, different from Golubic training --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you told us that, sir.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I thought it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us that.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- police training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was asking specifically about descending a rope on a rock face, and your answer is that that is police training, not military training?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier, I didn't climb down a rope on a rock face, so it could be police training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to Udbina. You testified that you were thrown out by the JNA from Udbina, and that Milan Martic and Milan Babic tried to negotiate but you were still thrown out. That was because you were not engaged in classical police training, as you called it, there but you were in fact engaged in military and combat training, isn't it? And that's why you were thrown out by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is simply not possible. Twenty men in the face of an army that had helicopters, tanks, armoured vehicles, we did not represent any danger at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't suggesting that you represented a danger to the JNA. What I was suggesting is that the JNA didn't want you there conducting combat and military training, and that's why you were thrown out; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained what kind of training we had. Why they drove us out, I cannot answer that. You should ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you give -- you were there. Can you give us any possible reason why the JNA would throw you out if you were simply engaged in classical police training and there simply so that the trainees could go home and visit their families? Why would the JNA do that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why. I wondered, too. We did not represent any danger. Our unit was small and disciplined, and we did not represent any danger. I cannot think of any reason. I did not attend those negotiations and talks with army officers. We just received an order to withdraw to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified, going back to Golubic, that you heard that one of your colleagues in Golubic slapped some Croat prisoners and that Captain Dragan summoned Mr. Martic and asked him, "How long are we going to tolerate things of this kind," and that Mr. Martic then expelled the commander. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we also corrected it a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, there was some question about what was meant by what Captain Dragan said. But you didn't tell the end of the story, did you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which end?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in fact, the commander who was expelled was allowed to stay at Golubic, wasn't he? He was not -- the order was not enforced. He was allowed to stay, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that on that day I was probably at home or maybe in Knin somewhere, and later --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- my friends told me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know from your friends that he was allowed to stay, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My friends told me that Mr. Martic was there and expelled him. I don't know what became of him later, and I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to read -- I'm going to read to you from the summary of your evidence that was provided to us by the Defence, by the Defence counsel, and this is what they said you would testify about. And it says: "On one occasion, a few Croatian prisoners were brought to Golubic. One of the instructors physically attacked them. Captain Dragan informed Milan Martic about the incident and Martic ordered that the instructor be expelled from the camp. However, the trainees stood against the order, so he stayed, but he was strictly forbidden to approach the Croats." That's what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe we didn't yesterday -- I don't know his name. I mean, we did not deal with the whole issue. I was told that they sort of rebelled, "Why are you expelling the man? If he's going, we're going, too." And they sort of set a condition, and I think they maybe told me that he stayed. What became of that man later, I don't know. He may have stayed in Golubic, but probably under some conditions. But I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. Now, when I said -- now, I said I didn't know the man and I don't know what became of him later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, just a moment ago I asked you this question: "You know from your friends that he was allowed to stay, don't you?" And your answer was: "My friends told me that Mr. Martic was there and expelled him. I don't know what became of him later and I don't know his name." Now, that was a lie, wasn't it? In fact, you've now told us that you learned that the other trainees rebelled and that he was allowed to stay.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to say it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
