utterances.text: I want you to answer my question, sir. When you told us -- before I read to you what was in the summary of your testimony, you lied to this Court, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not lie, Mr. Prosecutor. I would have liked to have been there that day. Maybe I would have known the details better. But I'm telling you what I heard from others. They told me that they protested and that he stayed. But I don't know what became of him later and I'm telling you, I don't know who that man is. So it's possible that even he left after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they told me that they managed to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, you didn't tell us that yesterday, and when I asked you specifically if he was allowed to stay, you said, "I don't know what happened --" "I don't know what became of him." And that testimony simply was not true, was it? Because you do know that he was allowed to stay.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe we didn't go through the whole issue. I don't see the point. My colleagues told me that somebody slapped those people - I don't want to repeat the whole thing - and that Mr. Martic came and expelled him. But they asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want you to repeat it either. This whole story you know from your colleagues. You didn't see any of it, did you? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that on that day I was probably at home, somewhere in Knin, so I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you heard that this person had been expelled by Milan Martic and equally you heard that ultimately he was allowed to stay. You heard both those things; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard. And it was not my intention to lie to the Court. I have no reason to lie to the Court. Why would I lie? I have no reason to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You have no reason to lie to the Court, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to. Why would I?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now you can't tell us the name of the commander that was involved in this, who slapped the Croat prisoners and who was expelled and then not expelled? You can't tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Or is it that you don't want to tell us?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know his name. And it didn't interest me that much. It wasn't a commander. Maybe he was a commanding officer from some group, from some town, from -- what do I know? I really don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, are you just sort of making this up as you go along, your testimony? Because a moment ago it was a commander and now you're saying it wasn't a commander. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you said "commander." Commander and commanding officer is not the same. I said commanding officer yesterday and today, and you used the word "commander," which is a totally different concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk about the prison. You testified yesterday that some 15 or 20 men were sent from Golubic to transfer some Croat prisoners to the old hospital, and then you described the hospital this way, and I'm going to quote what you said. You said: "There were window panes shattered, doors broken. There was no hot water. I don't even know if there was cold water." That's at page 45 of yesterday's transcript. That was the condition that you found at the old hospital, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the old hospital consisted of two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- one when you entered the main gate --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- this was before you said that. You described the old hospital, and you said that the person in charge of your group complained that he had to provide security and try to fix up the old hospital at the same time. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, and then later you claimed - this is on page 53 - you later claimed that in fact there were one or two rooms that were habitable that the prisoners could stay in while you fixed up the hospital. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all the rooms were in the same condition. Some were more damaged; some less. And in every room some repairs needed to be done. In some, more; in some, less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, sir, you're telling us that even though you described -- you said there was no hot water. "I don't even know if there was cold water. But, in fact, there were one or two rooms where the windows were fine and there were doors and there was hot water." Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. You didn't understand me properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, explain, then, please. Or let me put it to you this way: Isn't it, in fact, the case that these were the conditions of the hospital and the prisoners lived in those conditions until they were fixed up? Isn't that really what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the prisoners were brought, I know they were put up in the right wing, half of which was occupied by labour medical people, some doctors and nurses. Right next to them were those abandoned rooms that had not been used for a couple of years. However, there were works that needed to be done in all of those rooms. In some, more; in some, less. In one, one window pane was shattered; in another one, five window panes were shattered. The water was available in that part. In the left wing, there was no water. I think I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, then, can you explain to me, if there was a part of the hospital, the rooms that were perfectly habitable, what was the urgency? Why was the commander of your group anxious about trying to provide security and fix up the hospital at the same time? If you had rooms that were fine, what was the urgency?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were things that needed to be done. It was not urgent, but they needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, when --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply that man worked very hard for three or four days. He wasn't coping and he came to ask for assistance. What's unusual about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, he came to ask for assistance and wasn't coping because the matter was urgent, wasn't it? Because the prisoners were being held in areas that were not, in fact, habitable, were they? That's why he needed assistance.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly the conditions were not like here. But, listen, we didn't have any better. We had what we had. But it was our wish to improve the conditions to the best possible level, to the maximum possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Can I interrupt? Can I get an answer to your question that the Prosecutor asked you and to which I have not received an answer to? You were asked that: These were the conditions of the hospital and the prisoners lived in those conditions until they were fixed up. And the conditions are the conditions that you were referred to, that you testified about yesterday - no window panes, no hot water, and doubting whether there was even cold water, and no doors. Do you remember that? Is it correct that these detainees lived in those conditions until they were fixed up -- before they were fixed up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said yesterday precisely that we elected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you? Can I interrupt you? I'm not asking you about what you said yesterday. I'm asking you now: Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that we chose the part where water was available. In the left wing, there was no water; in the right wing, there was water. No hot water, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you? Is it correct? That's my question. Answer my question. Don't formulate a question for yourself and answer it. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, in that case, would you please repeat the question. I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it correct that the detainees lived in those conditions until they were fixed up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what's so difficult in answering such a simple question? You're telling me about what happened yesterday, what you said yesterday. Why do you take so long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not taking a long pause after your question, but it's difficult to answer because the situation was complex. One needs to go back to that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, you're not answering my question. I'm not asking you about pausing after my question. I said: What makes it so difficult to answer such a simple question? Don't you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's difficult to answer a question with a "yes" or "no". And if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What makes it so difficult? If the question asks -- demands a "yes" or "no," what is so difficult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's because I wish to provide an explanation for you to understand why it was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't need an explanation. If I need it, I will ask for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you to answer a question. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in that last exchange, you did say, however, that where the prisoners were held there was no hot water; correct? In the right wing.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first three, four or five days, six on the outside, there was no hot water.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, by August of 1991, there were -- there was more than 50 prisoners being held at the prison in Knin; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were at which stage. Things changed from one day to the next, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the period --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: August of 1991, you were appointed the warden of this prison. There were approximately 50 prisoners in August of 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is there a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, there is an answer that was given at page 52, line 5. "No, the first three or four or five days, six on the outside, there was no hot water." I'm not quite understanding what "on the outside" means in that context. I just wondered whether that could be clarified. I'm not familiar with that term in that way. That's why. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I had understood it that way, too, as "at most six days."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. I was educated there. Thank you very much, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, once again, you have answered with "It's possible." Don't you know that there were -- when you were appointed warden of this prison, the most important position you ever held in your life, that there were 50 prisoners there, or approximately 50 prisoners at the prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know the exact number? I would have to look at a report as to how many there were. Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I said -- sir, if you listen carefully to my question, I said "approximately 50"; 48, 52, approximately 50.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. You said -- when I asked you that question earlier, you said, "It's possible." Is your answer now that, yes, there were approximately 50 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible there were around 20; it's possible there were around 50. Now I don't know how many there were in 1991 and how many there were in 1993 and then in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So when you say, "It's possible," really what you're saying is you have no idea?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sir, what was the capacity at that moment of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we skipped over that part. As the number of inmates increased, the right wing increased --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, no, no. What do you mean "we skipped"? Who is "we"? And what do you mean by "we skipped"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour it wasn't mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I asked you something. You don't have to comment on that question. Just answer that question, please. When you became the warden of this prison, what was the capacity of the prison? How many prisoners could the prison hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could hold even more than the number mentioned by this gentleman here. There were around 15 rooms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What was the capacity of that prison? How many prisoners could be held in the prison, according to the capacity at that time? Give me the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe around 100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So there was no official number? You cannot give us a number? You said, "Maybe around --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot off the cuff, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And you said there were 15 rooms? How many people per room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on the size of the room - they differed in size - there were rooms only slightly smaller than this so they could hold many more people. And, according to the rules of procedure, the rule was that 8 cubic metres had to be allotted at least to one inmate. Maybe 12. I cannot remember off the top of my head. I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did I just understand you, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You'll probably pick it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly to say that there were rooms in the hospital that were the size of the room you're sitting in right now? Is that what you just testified to?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not like this, but smaller. But very large. There were some smaller and some large. That used to be a hospital. A room would have 30 square metres; some 15; some 40. That's the sizes they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think maybe this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, yesterday you testified that you made sure that there was no unauthorized access to the prison by placing guards at the gates. This was at page 48 of yesterday's transcript. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know what you mean by "possibly," because last time you said "possibly," it turned out you had no idea. Do you want me to read the testimony to you from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have to read it for me. But the posting of outside security guards, outside the prison was mandatory, and it served to prevent unauthorized access to the prison and prevent anyone from leaving the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Read the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's at page 48. The question was: "Q. How exactly did you make sure that there would be no unauthorized access?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We placed guards on the gates and it was possible to ensure security." Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's exactly the way it was. But I would have said the same if you had asked me whether anyone could escape. But I just complemented my answer. That is true, what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, if you could just focus on what my question is, because I didn't ask anything about escape, and just answer that question, things will go much more quickly here. In fact, sir, at least at the beginning, the guards were unable to prevent people from the outside from entering the prison and sometimes insulting the prisoners and even attacking the prisoners, isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me read again from the summary of the evidence that was provided to us by the Defence. This is a summary of what your evidence would be. "The witness was sent to Knin to organise a prison in the building of the old hospital. Due to the fact the building was not constructed to be a prison, at the beginning the guards were unable to prevent people from the outside from entering the prison and sometimes insulting and attacking the prisoners." Now that I've read that, do you remember that that, in fact, happened at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that may have happened at the beginning, but you're asking me about a time when the district prison was set up, and you are reverting me to an earlier period. When the prison was formed, a metal gate was installed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's take this one step at a time. Is what I -- what I read, in fact, what happened? That: "The witness was sent to Knin to organise a prison in the building of the old hospital. Due to the fact that the building was not constructed to be a prison, at the beginning the guards were unable to prevent people from the outside from entering the prison and sometimes insulting and attacking the prisoners." That happened; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards were, as we said yesterday, from the Territorial Defence. They had their commanding officer. And they prevented anyone from going in. They could not always prevent people from going in. But when the district prison was formed, when the professionals started working there, that could no longer happen. There was no such possibility any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I make an appeal to you, sir, to please answer the questions that are put to you. Don't formulate your own questions and answer them. Please answer the question that is put to you. The question is: Those things that are mentioned, did they happen in the beginning? Your answer should rather be "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to say that from the time I became warden of the prison, such things did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you are not being asked about the time you became a warden. You are being asked about the beginning. That is a summary of a statement allegedly that was made on your behalf. That's what you told your lawyers you are going to tell us when you get here. Did you say to your lawyers that, in the beginning it was not possible to prevent people from coming in, attacking the prisoners, insulting them at times? Did you say that to your lawyers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no. Did you or did you not say so? You should know if you did say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what I said. I don't know whether I put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you didn't say it, where did your lawyers get it from? Why did the lawyers come to tell the Prosecution this is what you are going to say if that's not what you told them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I was clear. If you want me to repeat, I can do that. Whilst the Territorial Defence was there, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question is: Where do your lawyers get it from? Listen to the question. Where do your lawyers get this information from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They got it possibly -- how should I know where they got it from? I don't know where they got it from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, they say this is a summary of what you told them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I told them is exactly what I'm telling you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What you're telling me is not exactly what is said in that summary. Did you tell your lawyers that, in the beginning it was not always possible to prevent people coming in, insulting the prisoners and at times attacking them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, again, I ask you: Why does it take you so long just to give that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult to reply to a question with just a "yes" or "no." I just wanted to explain how things really were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you have done it. You have just said, "Da." It's very simple. What's difficult about that? You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us why -- before I read to you from the summary, I put to you the very same question, I said -- and it's at page 56 of the transcript. I said: "In fact, sir, at least at the beginning, the guards were unable to prevent people from the outside from entering the prison and sometimes insulting the prisoners and even attacking the prisoners; isn't that true?" And your answer was: "No, that is not true." However, now you have just told us that, yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No. This was a different question. Excuse me, Mr. Whiting. No. It was the question what witness has told his lawyers, and your question was referring directly to the -- to what happened on the ground at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I can try to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You have now told us that you told the lawyers that, at the beginning -- that in the beginning it was not always possible to prevent people coming in, insulting the prisoners and at times attacking them. You said yes, you told the lawyers that. And you told the lawyers that because that was true; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I said that, but when I said that, I was referring to the Territorial Defence period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir, please. What you told the lawyers was true; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now let me ask my question: Then why earlier, when I asked you -- this is at page 56, I asked you: "In fact, sir, at least at the beginning, the guards were unable to prevent people from the outside from entering the prison and sometimes insulting the prisoners and even attacking the prisoners; isn't that true?" Using word for word what's from -- the summary of your statement. And you said: "No, that is not true." Why did you give that answer, sir, when you are now telling us that it is true?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to tell me what -- what guards, and then I will tell you yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, that wasn't your answer to my question. When I put the question, you didn't ask me what guards. You simply said: "No, that is not true." Why is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is because I now had in mind the professionals who were taken on. When they started working, this did not happen. It was not possible for that to happen. I may have spoken in the other context, the 10 or 15 days before that time when the Territorial Defence were the guards, who did not know the job and they were inexperienced and simply could not prevent such things from happening. I believe that I am clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were the professional guards there in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten to 15 days prior to the establishment of the district prison in Knin, the rooms in which the detainees were secured by members of the Territorial Defence. And I said so yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will ask you again. Were the professional guards there in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What makes you then think of the professional guards? We're talking about the beginning, and the word "beginning" we take from you, from your summary. What makes you think of professional guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to know what period I'm referring to. I explained that for 10 to 15 days, it was the Territorial Defence, and then they were replaced by professional guards. So the two periods differ in that sense. That is what I tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know that in the beginning professional guards were not there, and you know that the question put to you relates to the beginning. Now, why do you think of professional guards in the beginning, when you know they were not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that I was clear. I fail to actually comprehend what it is that you're asking me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I repeat my question: You know that professional guards were not there in the beginning. You know that the question put to you relates to the beginning. Why do you think it would have been the professional guards who were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor did not tell me that this question referred to the beginning. He did not specify what exact period he was referring to. He just referred to the entry -- entries into the prison, access to the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, do you want us to show you, play you the transcript -- show you the transcript where the question was put?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's at page 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you look at page 56, line 18. That's when the question was first put to you by the Prosecutor. "In fact, sir" - I'm reading now what the question said - "at the beginning" - underline the word "beginning" - "the guards were unable to prevent people from the outside from entering the prison and sometimes insulting the prisoners and even attacking the prisoners; isn't that true?" Your answer was: "No, that is not true." And that word, "beginning," the Prosecutor tells the Chamber that he gets from the summary of your statement, and you have agreed with the question I put to you that that statement you told to your lawyers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when we say "the beginning," to me the beginning meant when the decision was taken for me to become prison warden and when the district prison in Knin was established. Did you mean that as the beginning, or the beginning ten days before that when the Territorial Defence was there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't know what you meant by "beginning." We just -- it's just been -- taking your word for it. You say in the beginning that's what happened, and the question is, did it happen in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the exact beginning needs to be defined for me. I cannot otherwise reply to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You should define it, because that's your word. But, in any case, we're not here for definitions. I was asking you a question -- let me just find out what my question was. Yes. My question to you is: Why do you think it's professional guards when you know professional guards were not there in the beginning? That's the question I am putting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot reply in any other way but to say that there were some instances that the Prosecutor mentioned during the period of the Territorial Defence. After them, there were no more such cases. And I believe that I am quite clear. I cannot give you a more precise answer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The phrase "Territorial Defence" has been used by you for the first time in relation to this whole question of the beginning. You just tell me -- you show us where the Prosecutor used the words "Territorial Defence," since he asked you that question at page 56, line 18.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor didn't mention that. I was precise. I don't know what other answer to give you. I referred to the period when this happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you say the Prosecution never mentioned Territorial Defence, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that the Prosecutor mentioned "Territorial Defence." I mentioned "Territorial Defence." And I referred also to the professional guards. And during the period of the Territorial Defence, there were such instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said: "I cannot reply in any other way but to say that there were some instances that the Prosecutor mentioned during the period of the Territorial Defence." Now, how you come to know that he mentioned incidents during the period of the Territorial Defence, how do you know that if he hasn't mentioned Territorial Defence or the period of Territorial Defence? Because he mentioned "beginning," "in the beginning."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just added -- I just explained what happened in which particular period. I said yes, in the affirmative, and I just added to that answer, that that happened while the Territorial Defence was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I get it on the record that you are not going to answer my question now? The question, why you think of professional guards, about the beginning. Or shall I take it that what you said earlier is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The beginning of the functioning of the district prison was then, when people were employed. That is what is the beginning for me. That is why I said to the Prosecutor that there had been no instances of such conduct, because that is what I meant by "the beginning."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's follow on from the period when the Territorial Defence was there. You were there, too, with the Territorial Defence, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what would have been so difficult about securing the entrances of the prison to prevent people from coming in to insult and attack the prisoners? Why couldn't that be done?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I explained yesterday, the Territorial Defence consisted of elderly people of about 50 years of age, who, until yesterday, had been storekeepers or doctors, and now that person should prevent a younger person from coming into the rooms? That was a difficult task. That is why it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You better be careful about how you describe elderly people. But putting that aside, sir, these members of the Territorial Defence had weapons, didn't they? They had guns; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did have weapons, but they did not dare use them. They were amateurs and they really didn't have it in them to shoot at anyone under such conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you're telling me that these men - I'll call them young men - from the Territorial Defence with weapons were unable to prevent people from coming in and attacking the prisoners? That's really your testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that they were old, but they were a bit advanced of age. Actually, what I said is that they were older than these other people who were younger, who were 20 or 30. So I apologise for any insult that may have been construed. But they were not able to prevent -- in many instances they were not able to prevent anyone from entering. In some cases they were able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that you stayed behind, of the 15 or 20 men from Golubic, you stayed behind. The others returned to Golubic because: "The new commanding officer from the Territorial Defence was not very experienced and he didn't feel capable of handling it himself, so I was asked to stay on and help out." That's at page 48. Now, with all due respect, sir, you didn't have any experience either, did you, at that time? You had no experience.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have experience, but I had been there for some ten days and I knew a bit more than he did. And perhaps I was a bit more courageous, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that it, that you were more courageous?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. Maybe slightly more than this commanding officer, who was scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But can you give us his name, sir? What was his name, this commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. His last name is Novkovic or Novakovic. It starts with a "N." I remember that before the war he worked in the same factory as I, but I don't remember his name exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is there another reason, sir, that you were left behind at the prison. Of that group from Golubic, is there another reason that you were chosen to stay behind?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No other reason. Just for me to stay on and help him out a bit so that he would gain -- acquire some self-assurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You then testified that you consulted with the Minister of Justice, whose Risto Matkovic, and you told him that you did not have the proper training or the qualifications for the job of warden, and that you didn't even want the job. All of those things were true; right? You didn't have the training, the qualifications for the job, and you didn't want it; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And yet he appointed you warden of the prison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday, he asked me to stay on until the professionals arrived and assumed those positions. And he said that we would very quickly find another arrangement --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to fill my position of warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the professionals arrived in August of 1991, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And among them, there were lots of candidates for warden, lots of people who could have been the warden; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not among those people. There were no candidates that could be wardens among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Really? Well, let's look at Exhibit 906, then, please. And if we could look at page 1 of the B/C/S and page 10 of the English. This is a document -- do you remember seeing this document yesterday? You looked at this document.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So number 3 is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does the Court have the English on the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're getting that. Number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You have the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Because I don't have it on mine for some reason, but that's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Number 3 is Jovica Novakovic. And, according to this, he started on the 17th of August, 1991, and he had previously worked at the Zagreb district prison. So he had experience that you didn't have; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let's look at page 2 of the B/C/S and page 11 of the English, and specifically at number 8. Ilija Gambiroza started working at the Knin district prison also on the 17th of August, 1991; previously worked in Sibenik district prison. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he worked as a guard in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look at the next page of the English. We stay on the same page of the B/C/S. And it's number 9. Zoran, I think it should be "Dzukic" but -- oh, no, Dukic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Dukic. He started working on the 17th of August, 1991. He completed the course for warden training in Zagreb and worked at the Zadar district prison before coming to the Knin district prison; right? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm not going to go through the entire list, but -- I will if you want to, but if you take my word for it, there are 21 names on this list of men who started in August or in the fall, who had -- who had taken courses in this field, who had worked in this field, worked in prisons before; 15 of those 21 started in August of 1991. So all of those men would have been better qualified to be the warden than you; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say so. I don't think they had better qualifications. They had experience in prisons, but they had worked as guards. This first one was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- named head of the guards or chief of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't have anything; you didn't have experience, you had never worked in a prison, you had not taken any courses, you had not worked as a policeman. You had your training at Golubic and that's all. Why were you better qualified than these 21 other men on this list?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not more qualified, but I was not less qualified either. I told you yesterday, a warden does not have to belong to that line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, you told us yesterday that you told Mr. Matkovic that you were not qualified, you were not trained, and you did not want the job. So why didn't he give it to one of these 21 other men who were -- who had more qualifications than you? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he didn't give the job to somebody else. You should ask him that question. But what I'm telling you is that none of the other men either were qualified, and we just left that issue for later. We thought we'd find a solution later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and we did, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- according to you, a solution wasn't found for some 15, 16 months, until October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, you testified -- as I understood your testimony yesterday, in maybe March or April, Mr. Nikola Kukavica was appointed the warden but he held it for a short time only, and that you then held the position until October of 1992 when Mr. Nikola Ljubojevic was appointed. So, in fact, you held the position until October 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that, but as I thought about it last night, it was not actually in October. This Nikola Kukavica, he used to be warden of the prison in Lepoglava, and that's true, from Croatia. And he was the final solution. He had all that was necessary to be warden of a prison. However, after a while, after, I don't know, several months or two months, he left. I think he went to Serbia to join his daughter. It doesn't matter. And then, by that time, I already had some experience, and the minister asked me to be in that position again until we find a different solution. I'm sorry. Maybe at the end of the day, maybe the minister believed that the prison was operating fine, and I really think its functioning was excellent and that may have been the reason why he appointed me. There was no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you were put in charge of the prison, instead of those 21 other men who had experience in prisons, precisely because of your association with Milan Martic, whom you said yesterday you knew very well - that's at page 27 - and because you had gone through the training at Golubic? Isn't that why you were put in charge of that prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that certainly isn't the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, how do you know that is certainly not the reason? When I asked you before what the reason was, you said you didn't know and that I would have to ask Mr. Matkovic. How do you know that is certainly not the reason?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I told you yesterday that Mr. Matkovic had invited me for a talk and I told him straight out that I'm not going to be warden, I had no ambitions to be warden, and he was not actually forcing me. He was just asking me to stay on until he found the proper person to fill that position, somebody who had already worked in a prison. He just asked me to stay on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And he wanted you to stay on because you were Milan Martic's man; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not insist. And when I suggested to him that we find a warden -- if he had found another warden the next day, he would have appointed him the next day. However, it took a while until he found Nikola Kukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, it was because you were in charge of the prison, you were the warden of the prison, that is why the SAO Krajina police could come into that prison and beat and abuse prisoners there. Isn't that so? Precisely because you were in charge.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm telling you again, nobody could enter the district prison in Knin. What is that supposed to mean? I was there. There were lots of people. I didn't know people from the police. Some people were employed who had been dismissed from elsewhere in Croatia, professional policemen. Who did I know there? Why? It doesn't make sense, I mean, what you're saying, that people were coming in to go into the prison just because I was there. It's beginning to be a little insulting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let's look at -- if we could look at page 12 -- at the same document, page 12 of the document in English, and it's the next page in B/C/S. And if we could zoom in on the top of the page where your name is, and you talked about this yesterday, and it says here -- one thing that we didn't talk about yesterday is, it says here that you have a total of eight years of service. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this document, just to be clear, this document -- the date of this document is the 19th of May, 1993. So, in fact, you had at that time -- the 19th of May, 1993, you had, at most, two years of service; isn't that true? Not eight years.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, years of service for the purpose of calculating a salary are calculated, under our law, to include years spent in other companies and enterprises. And I had already worked before in the bolts and screws factory, and that is included. So if you go to serve on another court, your years of service from here will also count.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So when it says "eight years of service," that means -- that means basically your working life, the number of years you've been working?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found a job for the first time in 1985, and that makes eight years, if the document is from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you were not -- I'm moving on to another topic. You testified that you were not happy with Jovica Novakovic because he did nothing to prevent or report maltreatment of prisoners by two guards. Who were the two guards involved in that incident?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that from memory. That happened in 1991. We had all those documents in the archive, but right now, off the top of my head, I cannot tell you the names of the guards. I know that disciplinary proceedings were instituted against them, as in other cases that came later, but I don't remember that. It was all duly put on record, but those records remained behind, just as our houses, that they burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I would suggest that that last part of your answer was not, in any way, responsive to my question. Now, you told Mr. Matkovic about this, right, that you wanted to replace Mr. Novakovic for this reason, because of what you had discovered; right? You reported that to Mr. Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was required to inform the minister. It was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question. My question wasn't what you were required to do or what your duty was to do. My question was what you, in fact, did. Did you do it? Did you report it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you found Mr. Tauz and you proposed Mr. Tauz to replace Mr. Novakovic. And you told that to Mr. Matkovic; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said to Mr. Matkovic earlier that I had heard of a man who had worked in Zadar before, who was highly professional, who enjoyed authority among his men, because there were some men who had worked with him in Zadar where he was a sergeant. I only heard of that man. I didn't know him. He lived in Zadar and I lived in Knin. And as soon as this happened, I suggested to Mr. Matkovic to employ him as chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Mr. Matkovic knew that the reason you wanted to employ Mr. Tauz as chief is because you needed to get rid of Mr. Novakovic for the reasons that you had explained; that he was not enforcing the rules in the prison; right? Mr. Matkovic knew all of that.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Tauz came, he insisted, did he not, that there be adequate documentation detailing the basis on which the prisoners were sent to the prison; right? That's something he insisted on.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remember something different. Maybe something similar happened, but that's not -- that was not the issue. If you want me to, I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, if your answer is you don't remember him insisting on that, then I will move on.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether he was able to or not, I don't know. I don't know what his conditions were that he said -- laid down before the minister. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. When you say he insisted, are you meaning that -- do you mean that these were the conditions precedent to him taking on the job? Or having taken the job, he insisted on these things being put in place?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The former, Your Honour, that he insisted -- that this was a condition -- before accepting the job he insisted -- or as can condition of accepting the job, adequate documentation detailing the basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, sir, there were civilians who were being taken and held in that prison as war prisoners; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was not interested in who was civilian or not. All I was interested in was a decision of the competent court that somebody be imprisoned. Whether they were civilians or not, I wasn't interested in knowing. We admitted people only on the basis of court decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I want to focus on -- you described yesterday how there were different categories of prisoners and one category was war prisoners. And you are aware that in the fall of 1991 there were civilians among those war prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I didn't want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't want to know.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the competent court or a competent institution issues a decision to have somebody imprisoned, all I wanted was to have a decision on what grounds we were to admit him into the prison. I was not interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 909, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't think that's it, 9 -- I'm sorry, I misspoke. I meant to say "919". I'm sorry. I said "909" and I meant to say "919".

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this is a list of prisoners, and I want to draw your attention to number 204, Mijo Bacic. Do you see his date of birth is the 28th of January, 1920, which means that he was 71 years old on the date he was arrested. Do you remember him, a 71-year-old man? You were the warden of the prison. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I'm not doubting your words. I don't remember the man, but I mean I don't have to remember one person in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you don't remember this 71-year-old man?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, my English exhibit just disappeared and then a specious one appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, if we could have the English on the English screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, now it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, maybe you don't remember this man by his name, but do you remember men of that age, 70 years old, being held, being taken prisoner, being brought to your prison as prisoners in October and November of 1991? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that specifically, but I'm not saying that he was not brought to the prison. It's possible. If he's on the list, then it's sure that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, isn't that -- isn't that something that would kind of stand out, some 70-year-old man being brought in and held as war prisoners? Isn't that something you might have noticed?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, he could have been one 120 years old. If the municipal or district court issued a decision to imprison him, it meant nothing to me that he was 70 years. You may have people imprisoned in The Hague who are 70 or 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, so what you're telling us is that as long as somebody of authority was doing something, you would turn a blind eye to it and you would not make your own judgement about it? Is that what you're telling us? As long as they had the proper documentation or the proper authority to do something, it's not your business to get involved; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's take, for example, the district court issued a decision, a verdict --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to imprison that man, what was I supposed to do, come to the district court and protest?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to get to that. But you're not answering my question, you're giving me an example. My question was: As long as somebody had the proper documentation or the proper authority to do something, you decided it wasn't your business to get involved and you would not get involved. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's just look at -- there are a number of examples in this document, but I do want to look at one more, which is at page 6 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. It's number 236 on the list. Do you see there number 236, Bozo Plazanic, born in 1905; 86 years old, if my math is right. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't remember clearly the face of the man, but I know, in that period, there were some elderly people and I know they were released. And you can see that in the last column, where you see "released" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct. They were released six days later. They were arrested on the 13th of November, 1991, and they were held for six days and then they were released. Do you remember that man? Do you remember that group of -- that man and the other elderly men that were held there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that he was there. I don't doubt that he was there. But he was eventually released and he wouldn't have been released if we did not have the appropriate decision, because we did everything according to decisions, as I told you. Why he was put in prison in the first place, I don't know. Maybe the security situation was bad in the territory where he lived. Maybe he assisted somebody in something. One should have to look at the decision why he was imprisoned. But we see here that he was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, did you think that this 86-year-old man was a proper war prisoner, was a combatant? Did you think that at the time? Bearing in mind what you told us about the Territorial Defence men who were 50 years old and their capabilities.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what was in my mind or wasn't in my mind did not matter to anybody. What mattered was the decision of the appropriate institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, it matters to me, which is why I have put the question to you. So if you could answer the question: Did you think that this 86-year-old man was a combatant?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think about that and I cannot answer you now. I don't know what to answer to your question, whether I thought about it. I didn't. I had a thousand other things I had to do. I couldn't think of whether he should be there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you were the warden of the prison.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll move on. You testified that -- when you were talking about discipline, you testified that the disciplinary options that were available to you were reprimand, fine, suspension and dismissal, and that as the warden you had the last word. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you decided, then, that even though Jovica or is it -- sorry. I'm not sure. Is it Jovica or Jovan? Novakovic, Mr. Novakovic, even though he had failed to report this abuse of prisoners and had done nothing about it, it was your decision that he could stay on in the prison, continue to be employed in the prison, and that he could even have a supervisory role. That was your decision; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said yesterday that the warden and the chief were appointed by the minister, and the minister can also recall whoever he appoints. So the warden could complain to the minister that the chief was not working well, but he couldn't replace him. He could only complain to the minister, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could institute disciplinary proceedings against all other staff members except the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But yesterday you told us that he was suspended, so there were disciplinary proceedings against him. So my question is: Why wasn't he dismissed? Why was he allowed to continue working in the prison? Why wasn't he dismissed, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was suspended, but he was suspended by the minister. Why he reinstated him, I can only assume. I can only assume that it was because he was the only one with that rank, and we didn't want to remain without the one person with that rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we had five or six sergeants --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask, what rank do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sergeant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk about the rank, because yesterday you testified that he could not be demoted in terms of his rank, and that rank was something that was acquired in schooling, in school. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at Exhibit 906 again, please, and we need to look at page 10 of the English and page 1 of the B/C/S. Could we have page -- thank you. I want to look, in particular, at number 3, Jovica Novakovic, a man we have just been talking about. Let's look at what his schooling was. He finished primary school in Vrhovine and secondary wood-processing school, and then he went to a two-year college of wood processing in Zagreb. His vocation is listed as a wood industry engineer. And he finished three years of faculty of communications. So can you explain to me, how is it that he obtained the rank of sergeant from his schooling?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in Zagreb, as you can see. I don't know how he was conferred that rank in Zagreb. He has a higher education degree and he probably passed some specialistic exams for the title of supervisor. I really don't know what else he may have completed. He just brought his documents showing that he was this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in fact -- and I'm going to -- if I can find my pile. If I could just have a moment. I need to look at two different documents at once, and so I am going to pass out what's Exhibit 905 - keep this exhibit on the screen, and pass out, by hard copy, with the assistance of the usher, 905.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the interpreters could be provided with copies. There is no text, it is just names, actually, so it shouldn't be a difficulty.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: All right, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that we were looking at -- I'm sorry, I think you have an English version, but it is just the names and I don't know if Defence counsel has a B/C/S version available to provide to the witness. It's Exhibit 905. I think I failed to print a B/C/S version of it. But it's just the names, really, that we're interested in. This is a document we were looking at yesterday when you started to talk about rank, because you said you were trying -- you were explaining why Mr. Novakovic was still listed as a guard supervisor, and you said, "Well, that's his rank --" I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, colleague. I don't have this document, but this is -- right now, but this is the document that we saw yesterday. Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And I again apologise for not having it, but we will try to make do. If the witness needs to see the B/C/S version, we can put it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in fact, this doesn't refer to ranks, does it? It refers to positions in the gaol. Guard supervisor is not a rank, it's a position.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guard supervisor is a rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I thought you told us that the rank was sergeant, that his rank was sergeant. You just told us that a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sergeant. No, sorry, supervisor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No. Sorry, this was what you replied to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Supervisor is the rank. Perhaps I confused it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I asked you that question, do you remember? What was his rank? You answered "Sergeant." Try not to confuse us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. There are no sergeants. In prison the term is supervisors of the guards. I may have made a mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, are you just -- sir, are you just making this up as you go along? When you're shown a document, just responding like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And why are you smiling in this way? Did I say anything? Do you wish to say something with your smiling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please try to be serious.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. Your Honours, I may have provoked some laughter because it was a slip of the tongue. I was wrong when I said "sergeant."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I was referring to your expression of your face, not any others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have this expression, a smiling expression, when I am angry with myself, and I am angry with myself for having made this mistake. It was my own mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in fact, if you look at Exhibit 905, which is the list that you have in front of you, according to Exhibit 906 that we have on the screen, nearly all the men who are listed as guards have more schooling in the area of prisons and many have more experience in the area of prisons than Mr. Novakovic, and yet they are guards and he is a guard supervisor. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain that, Mr. Prosecutor. Under the then valid law, supervisor of the guards could be only a person with a higher educational degree, which is to say at least two years of schooling after secondary school. Persons with such a degree could take the exam for a guard's supervisor. If you look at these other cases, they all only had completed secondary schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, here's the problem with that answer. Let's look at the other men who are listed as guard supervisors. For example, Ilija Tauz, and you can see his name on the screen there as number 2, and let's look at his education. Finished primary school in Kistanje and secondary school of administration in Zadar. No schooling after secondary school. So what you just told us, that "only a person with a higher educational degree, which is to say at least two years of schooling after secondary school, could be a supervisor of the guards," that doesn't seem to be true, does it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. Under serial numbers 1 and 2, Orlovic and Tauz, these are people who had worked in Croatia, in prisons. So the practice was, if one was just a few years away from retirement and was a good professional, the possibility was allowed for persons with just secondary education to be promoted by the minister to the rank of supervisor. That possibility existed, and it was the practice in many areas of the former Yugoslavia. But a younger person could not obtain that rank without having the proper educational qualifications. The two people that you referred to were already retired, and they were retired in that rank. And as we needed such personnel, we didn't make any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, what is the age of retirement? What was the age of retirement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, they had privileged years of pensionable service, so that theirs was an early retirement. And this referred to the police and to prison staff, prison guards. They went into retirement much earlier than people working in a factory, say. They had privileged pensionable years of service, three or four months per year, depending on the actual institution. So they would be retired around the age of 45 or 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And by the two people that you are referring, who got their retirement on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two people under serial numbers 1 and 2 in the first group, Ilija Tauz and Jovo Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, number 1 is not -- I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm still marvelling at that. According to my list, number 1 is not Jovo Orlovic. Ilija Tauz, yes, is number 2. But number 1 is Nikola Ljubojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think he is referring to 905, the hard copy list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I beg your pardon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On 906, just for the benefit of the Court, Jovo Orlovic is number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you say -- when were they retired? What year were they retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were retired, I'm not sure, I believe in 1990. It was early retirement. Actually, some were retired and some were expelled. Those who fulfilled the pension requirements were pensioned off. I don't know. This happened in Croatian cities, in Zadar and elsewhere. But they had these ranks, the ranks that are indicated -- the tiles that are indicated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You realise that in 1990, Orlovic was just 41, not even 45 yet, and Tauz was even younger than that; he would have been 39.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the Croats drove them out, chucked them out. If circumstances had remained normal, they wouldn't have been retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So they did not retire because of this preferential treatment of accumulating service time in the police force. They were retired because they were chucked out. Which is which now? You have just told us that the pension scheme in the police is different from in the factories. You could accumulate days and months, three months in a year. Now you are saying, "No, no, no, they were chucked out." Which is correct between these two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, according to what they told me, they still needed to work for several years until retirement. But being Serbs, they simply had to leave their positions in Croatian prisons. Some were sent into early retirement; some others were simply chucked out. A number of prison guards, for instance, were simply chucked out from working in prisons in Croatian towns; in Zagreb, in Sibenik, in Zadar and in other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question? Thank you for that long speech. Answer my question, now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I say, they were pensioners, but we took them on because we were short of such personnel, to help us out. I'm referring to these two persons. They were already pensioners, but we asked them to come and work for us to help us out, because we did not have professionals with their kind of knowledge. And they accepted to come and work for us. Is that what you asked me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, I ask you to please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please be so kind as to repeat it? I thought that this was the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind as to listen when I ask the question? My question to you is: You've told us that there were preferential retirement schemes within the police force which is different from the factory; hence people could retire early. Now you've also told us that they retired early because they were chucked out from the Croatian police force. I'm saying: Which of those two is true? That's my question. Why do you give us two versions? And I'm saying, which one of these two versions is true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first version, that was the rule, that was the law. That was the procedure under the law. The second version refers to just these two men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have not. Which of these two versions is true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both versions are true. Those who were 39 or 40 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have something better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I am telling you all the while. They still needed three or four or five years of service to be retired. Had they -- they would have been 45 after such years had expired. Had they been working in a factory, they would have had to work for another eight or ten years or so, until sixty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have gone past the time. Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break, an adjournment. The case will proceed tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
